content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies a self-supervised strategy for molecular representations, called MOLBART. It is inspired by BART from the natural language processing domain which is a denoising model encoder-decoder architecture. The authors scaled the model training to a sizer larger than previous molecular representation models and conducted ablation studies to show that factors such as learned tokenization, bigger model size and certain training hyperparameters (including receipes) improve MOLBART’s representations for downstream tasks, achieving new state of the art results on 11 tasks. An interpretability method (integrated gradients) was used on Ames and ESOL to show that representations learned correlated with knowledge of domain experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
State-of-the-art results on 11 tasks
Ablation studies to show the source of model performance

Weakness:
-Limited novelty: model performance largely relies on existing strategies, with lack of algorithmic or modeling innovation
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are some parts of the paper that could benefit from more clarity:

“Masking Strategy in Objective”: regarding the randomize_tokens, what exactly happens for the 50% of the cases, is <mask> used as the random_mask mentioned or are tokens randomly substituted with other tokens from the vocabulary?

Table 2: What is the “AUC” based on?
content.summary_of_the_review: While the results in the paper have achieved state-of-the-art performance on some tasks, there is limited technical novelty in the paper to justify acceptance in such a venue. Hence, the reviewer is inclined toward a reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents BART model pre-trained on a billion-scale Zinc20 dataset and benchmarks that on property prediction and reaction prediction. The paper applies distributed training and uses large compute to train the model on a billion plus a  chemical SMILES and designs ablation experiments to dissect contribution of different components (tokenization, model size, compute, finetuning, masking).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The idea of learning molecular representation using large-scale pre-training on large number of chemical SMILES, while not new, is timely and targets important research problems. 
Design of ablation experiments is nice. 
The paper considers both property prediction and reaction prediction. 

Weaknesses:
The paper seems to be incomplete at its current state. E.g., no details of the generative tasks or results can be found in the manuscript. It is not clear whether the results on ablation experiments (Fig 1 and Tables 1-2) report an average over HIV, BBBP, and ClinTox or is for one out of these three. The classification performance does not appear as outperforming existing baselines on most of benchmarks (Authors seem to miss that the MoLFormer baseline uses scaffold split on all classification tasks “Table 3 documents the performance comparison of MOLFORMER with these pre-trained/self-supervised baselines on six classification benchmarks, while using scaffold data splits.” from arXiv:2106.09553). There seems to be major flaws in reporting the model performance -- the average reported in Table 4 does not equal to the average of RMSE of three regression tasks.  While Table 3 claims model is SOTA on Sider and Tox21, the text says otherwise.
content.summary_of_the_review: The details of the method and results presented in the paper are not strong enough to support the claim that the paper has discovered a robust self-supervised strategy for learning molecular representation toward prediction and generation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a generative masked language model called MolBART for molecular representations. Based on the representations, this paper uses some quantitative and qualitative methods to analyse them.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1) Strengths are described as follows:

a) This paper introduces a pre-trained model for molecular representations.

b) The experiments presents promising results for some downstream tasks.

2) Weaknesses are listed below:

  a) The authors didn’t interpret similarities or differences between the proposed model and other pre-trained models. 

b) The method is unclear. As we all know, implementations on MLM tasks are different between natural language and molecular SMILES. The authors ignore the indispensable demonstration such as how to do masking on molecules. Apart from that, there is no statement on how to operate each neuron in Section 5.1.

Questions:

1. How do the authors perform masking to molecules?
2. Why choose different baseline models and different sample sizes on different tasks without any consistency? 
3. What is the reason for doing a comparison on the randomly initialized model, does the initialization also a variable for the experiment in Table 1?
4. Why just perform the grid search only on the first four tasks in section 4.1.1? 
5. What is the supporting detail for the statement that MolBART is trained with an order of magnitude more compute than previous pre-trained molecular representations?
6. What is the real experimental result for training a single multi-task classification model with a significantly worse result stated in Section 4.1.1?
7. What is the tokenization method used in baseline models for comparison? Is the method the same as MolBART?
8. What is the clear split operation as the authors stated, “if we believe the authors used a different split” in Section 4.2?

c) The code or the trained parameters are not open-source, making this paper hardly reproducible.

d) The experimental result is not convincing. In Section 3, the authors state that they are unable to do a proper grid search so they choose another strategy. In Table 3, MolBART didn’t accomplish state-of-the-art performances on Tox21, HIV, BACE and BBBP. Compared to the baselines, the model didn’t achieve a significant improvement on datasets.

e) The comparison with baselines is incomplete, and the authors did not explain why. In Section 4.2, table (a), table (b) and table (c) are incomplete. Table (a) misses the ChemBERTa baseline, which had been shown in Table3. Table (b) and Table (c) only present results of a few baselines. 

f) Minor observations:

The numbers for figures and tables are in chaos, such as the tables in Section 4.2.

Some sentences do not seem grammatically correct, like “higher is better”, “we select using a learned tokenizer for the rest of our experiments.”

The paper is badly organized. For example, the authors didn’t point out the weaknesses of previous works and how they solved those problems, leading to a lack of novelty in this paper. The authors just pile up one study after another without an evaluative stance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces MolBART, a BART model trained on 1.7Bn SMILES of molecules. The paper's contributions are threefold. First, it details hyper-parameter decisions to train the pre-trained model, in particular vocabulary and masking strategy. Due to the very different distribution of SMILES and natural language, the authors show that the default hyper-parameter choices of BART are not optimal for MolBart. Second, it fine-tunes and evaluates the MolBART on regression, classification and generation tasks including MoleculeNet. The results are quite inconsistent in this section, with very important gains on some tasks while on others the model performs worse than simple baselines. Finally, the authors analyse the quality of the learned representations by showing that a few neurons suffice to get strong performance on some tasks and that attribution interpretability methods show the model highlights structures that correspond to what chemists have identified as important.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Section 3 (and Fig 1 in particular) is interesting and helpful. Often authors will gloss over these details and I appreciate this section being present, particularly since it adapts a method to a new domain.
- The proposed model is trained on significantly more data than prior approaches. With major caveats below, it seems to achieve very high performance on some tasks. It could be a good asset for the community. 
- Section 5.2 is interesting, though it would have been much better if it led the authors to try ablations with different pre-training datasets.

Weaknesses:
Most of the weaknesses and improvement suggestions relate to Section 4. Due in part to the numerous experiments and limited space for this section, some important information is lacking. In addition, there are clear errors. Currently, it it is a collection of results from which it is hard to extract a cohesive story. Improving this section and adding some of your own ablations would make this a much stronger paper. This is critical and warrants moving other sections to the appendix if you need the additional space.
- Ablations: It would be great to have more results from your own models on these tasks, especially given some of the issues mentioned below. For instance, a smaller MolBART, a MolBART trained on the smaller dataset of one of your baselines. Right now there are large, inconsistent differences in results across tasks between your model and other approaches and nothing to bridge this gap.  These ablations would also enable you to test your hypothesis of Sec 5.2 that Zinc20 is hurting your performance on Ames/Micronucleus. 
- Please comment a bit more on your ClinTox number. Is there anything in your setup/the dataset that would explain such strong gains? The improvement is surprisingly high, reducing the gap to a perfect score by 93% over the prior best number and basically solving the task. Other datasets do not show similar improvements. 
- Similarly, your regression numbers are excellent compared to prior results, with huge MSE reductions. Can you share some context as to what explains such strong improvements. The current explanation "Our model produced state-of-the-art results on all three regression tasks of the MoleculeNet suite" is not very insightful. 
- For your regression column, the "Avg" column does not seem to be an average. In fact, for MolBART, the average is less than half of the minimum. For other rows, the results also do not match up. 
- It would be easier if you reminded readers of key characteristics of some of the baseline methods. For instance text-based vs graph-based, # model parameters, and pretraining dataset size. 
- For HIB/BACE/BBBP and models that use the same splits (i.e not marked with *), how do you explain that MolBART performs relatively poorly?
- (Minor) Bolding of results: I would bold results on HIV/BACE/BBBP for other models when these use standard splits. On b) and c), it is inconsistent to bold your results but not the same numbers earlier in the table (FP Pubchem SVM). In Table 4, you should bold Transformer and MolBart Sample + Rerank on MIT (M). 


Spelling/writing/misc:
"the two toxicology datasets that direct fine-tuning" p6
Please make sure citation format is used correctly. For instance end of p2 for PyTorch and FairSeq citations, Lewis et al p3, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity and quality is poor on the results section (esp. 4.2) and better elsewhere. Unfortunately section 4.2 is critical to this paper.
* Novelty is limited, though I do not think this is the main issue with this paper.
* Due to some of the aforementioned weaknesses, I think reproducibility will be low.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has an interesting premise and some strong sections. However, the results section is quite poor and does not explain important inconsistencies in performance across tasks. The lack of ablations in this section makes it very hard to understand and evaluate the results.

content.title: MolBART: Generative Masked Language Models for Molecular Representations
content.TL;DR: We develop self-supervised representations of molecules using generative masked language models that set state-of-the-art for many chemical property and reaction prediction tasks and implicitly learn features and substructures important in chemistry
content.abstract: We discover a robust self-supervised strategy tailored towards molecular representations for generative masked language models through a series of tailored, in-depth ablations. Using this pre-training strategy, we train MolBART, a BART-like model with an order of magnitude more compute than previous self-supervised molecular representations. In-depth evaluations show that MolBART consistently outperforms other self-supervised representations across classification, regression, and generation tasks setting a new state-of-the-art on 10 tasks. We then quantitatively show that when applied to the molecular domain, the BART objective learns representations that implicitly encode our downstream tasks of interest. For example, by selecting seven neurons from a frozen MolBART, we can obtain a model having performance within two percentage points of the full fine-tuned model on task Clintox. Lastly, we show that standard attribution interpretability methods, when applied to MolBART, highlight certain substructures that chemists use to explain specific properties of molecules.
